about.title: San Mateo Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: A workday in San Mateo can put you on a loading dock off S El Camino Real, behind the wheel on US-101, or on a scaffold above a job site near SR-92. When something goes wrong, most people assume workers' compensation is the whole story. Often it is: California makes comp the usual exclusive remedy against your employer, and fault does not matter. Comp covers medical care and part of lost wages. If someone outside your company caused the harm — a subcontractor, the owner of the property where you were working, the maker of a tool that failed, or another driver who hit your work vehicle — a separate third-party injury claim may be open to you. That claim can address losses comp never touches. In San Mateo County, the two paths run side by side, and the timing matters: tell your employer within 30 days, and third-party claims carry a two-year deadline. LawProactive is not a law firm. We connect you, at no cost, with an independent attorney who handles these cases on contingency.

items.desc: You have 30 days to report the injury to your employer, and a third-party claim in California must be filed within two years. Getting connected early keeps both clocks in view.

items.desc: California law forbids employers from punishing you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. The independent attorneys we connect you with work on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I drive for work on US-101 through San Mateo and another driver hit me. Do I have one claim or two?
items.answer: Possibly two. Because you were on the job, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your wages no matter who was at fault. Because another driver caused the crash, you may also have a separate third-party injury claim against that driver. San Mateo recorded 386 injury collisions in 2025, and work trips make up a share of them, so this situation is not unusual.

items.question: My employer says I can only file for workers' comp. Is that true?
items.answer: Against your employer, comp is generally the exclusive remedy in California, so in that narrow sense they are right. But the rule protects the employer, not outside parties. If a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment manufacturer contributed to your injury, a third-party claim may still be available. An attorney can sort out which is which.

items.question: I was hurt on a job site near SR-92 but waited to report it. Is it too late?
items.answer: Report it now. California asks you to notify your employer within 30 days, and a prompt written report keeps your comp claim on solid footing. A third-party claim carries a separate two-year deadline, so even a delayed start does not necessarily close that door. Talking with an attorney soon helps clarify where you stand.
